description: Cervical region morphology: neck length and thickness, cervicomental angle, laryngeal prominence, sternocleidomastoid visibility, posterior neck. Dimensions are drawn from craniofacial anthropometry (Farkas) and cervicofacial-aesthetics literature (Ellenbogen-Karlin, Connell). The cervicomental angle is the central aesthetic landmark of the neck region; laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) is sex-dimorphic.

reliability_studies.method: test-retest: the identical prompt re-read against stored codings, same model, no human rater
reliability_studies.measures: reproducibility, NOT validity. Agreement between two readings says the instrument is stable, not that it is correct.
reliability_studies.corpus: publicly documented portraits of notable people, 39 ethnic groups, single frontal or three-quarter images
reliability_studies.statistic: percent agreement and Cohen's kappa over portraits where both readings gave a non-decline value
reliability_studies.decline_handling: A value meaning "could not assess" (unclear, not_visible, not_assessable, obscured, covered_unclear, not_applicable_or_*) is treated as a decline, not an answer. Scoring declines as answers makes a dimension that is never visible look perfectly reliable.
limitations: One model, one corpus, one re-read. No human inter-rater study exists for this vocabulary.

Kappa is fragile wherever one value dominates. Measured on this corpus: six dimensions read kappa at or below zero on 78 portraits and between 0.43 and 0.66 on 196, and every one has chance agreement above 85 percent. Those carry estimate_is_fragile and should be read as a band, not a number.
Notable-people corpora skew older and are not a population sample.
A dimension can be perfectly reproducible and still not measure what its name claims.

dimensions.scale_citation: Farkas LG (1994). Anthropometry of the Head and Face, 2nd Edition. Reference: cervical length (gnathion to suprasternal notch) proportional to overall facial height.
dimensions.description: Vertical neck length proportional to face height.

values.definition: Neck length less than approximately 70% of facial height.
Neck length approximately 70-100% of facial height (Farkas reference range).
Neck length substantially greater than facial height; swan-neck appearance.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with sports-medicine descriptors of cervical-girth norms; reference values vary substantially with sex and training.
dimensions.description: Neck thickness relative to head width.

values.definition: Neck substantially narrower than head; minimal cervical musculature.
Neck width proportional to head width.
Neck width approaches or exceeds head width; pronounced cervical musculature or subcutaneous fullness.

dimensions.scale_citation: Ellenbogen R, Karlin JV (1980). Visual criteria for success in restoring the youthful neck. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 66(6): 826-837. Reference: cervicomental angle 105-120° as the youthful aesthetic norm.
dimensions.description: Angle between the submental plane and the anterior neck.

values.definition: Crisp angular transition between submental plane and neck; aesthetic ideal.
Within Ellenbogen-Karlin reference range.
Reduced angle definition; common with submental fat or platysmal banding.

dimensions.scale_citation: Anatomic descriptor aligned with otolaryngology and gender-affirming-care literature on thyroid-cartilage prominence (chondrolaryngoplasty references).
dimensions.description: Visibility of the thyroid cartilage prominence. Sex-dimorphic — typically more prominent in adult-male physiognomy due to differing thyroid-cartilage angles.

values.definition: Thyroid cartilage barely visible; typical of female adult physiognomy.
Visible but not pronounced thyroid cartilage.
Pronounced Adam's apple; typical of male adult physiognomy.
Substantial thyroid-cartilage projection.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with surface-anatomy descriptors used in sports medicine and aesthetic-medicine literature.
dimensions.description: Visibility of the sternocleidomastoid muscle as a distinct surface landmark.

values.definition: SCM not discernible at the skin surface; soft-tissue coverage obscures muscle outline.
SCM faintly visible during rotation or tension.
SCM clearly visible at rest as a distinct landmark.
Pronounced SCM definition; very low body-fat percentage in the cervical region.

reliability.note: Chance agreement is high because one value dominates this corpus, so kappa is computed on a small (1 - pe) denominator and the estimate moves a long way on a few cells. Measured: between a 78-portrait and a 196-portrait read of the same corpus, dimensions in this regime moved by up to 0.68 of a kappa point, in both directions. Read the band, not the digits.

dimensions.scale_citation: Connell BF, Shamoun JM (1997). The significance of digastric muscle contouring for rejuvenation of the submental area of the face. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 99(6).
dimensions.description: Visibility of platysmal bands — the vertical neck cords that become more visible with aging or low body-fat percentage.

values.definition: Platysmal cords barely visible at rest.
Visible cords at rest; aging-related change.
Pronounced cords creating a 'turkey-wattle' appearance.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with the Connell-Shamoun and Ellenbogen-Karlin neck-aesthetics descriptors.
dimensions.description: Skin quality in the cervical region — common site for visible aging changes.

values.definition: Some texture or fine lines visible.
Visible cervical skin laxity; redundant skin folds.
Pronounced cervical wrinkles or 'necklace lines'.

references: Farkas LG (1994). Anthropometry of the Head and Face, 2nd Edition. Raven Press.
Ellenbogen R, Karlin JV (1980). Visual criteria for success in restoring the youthful neck. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 66(6): 826-837.
Connell BF, Shamoun JM (1997). The significance of digastric muscle contouring for rejuvenation of the submental area of the face. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 99(6).
